data.text/markdown: In this tutorial, we illustrate the sparse coding example in the Section 4.1 of the paper: Exact Verification of First-Order Methods via Mixed-Integer Linear Programming. Consider the following problem of recovering the signal ||(z^\star||): from its noisy measurement ||(x = D z^\star + \varepsilon \in {\bf R}^p||): ||[\begin{array}{ll} \text{minimize} & (1/2) \lVert Dz - x \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert z \rVert_1, \end{array}||]where ||(D \in {\bf R}^{p \times n}||) is the dictionary matrix, ||(\varepsilon \in {\bf R}^p||), ||(\lambda > 0||) is a sparsity-inducing regularization parameter, ||(z \in {\bf R}^n||) is the decision variable, and ||(x \in {\bf R}^p||) is the problem parameter. This problem can be solved with ISTA and its accelerated variant FISTA. We provide the definition of ISTA iteration below: ||[\begin{array}{ll} s^{k+1} = {\cal T}_{\lambda \eta} ( (I - \eta D^T D) s^{k} + \eta D^T x), \end{array}||]where ||({\cal T}_{\lambda}||) is a soft-thresholding operator applied element-wisely.

For the strongly convex example, we choose ||(p=20||) and ||(n=15||), and for the nonstrongly convex example, we choose ||(p = 15||), ||(n = 20||), and ||(\lambda = 10^{-1}||). To construct ||(D||), we randomly sample from i.i.d. Gaussian ||({\cal N}(0, 1/p)||) the ||(20||)% nonzeros of ||(D||) and normalize its columns. The true signal ||(z^\star||) is constructed by sampling each entry from i.i.d. Gaussian ||({\cal N}(0, 1)||) with probability ||(0.1||) and setting ||(0||) otherwise. We sample ||(m = 100||) of those random sparse signals ||(z^\star||). Finally, we let the parameter set ||(X||) to be the tightest hypercube containing all ||(x||)'s.

For the algorithm, we also choose ||(\eta = 1/L||), where ||(L||) is the maximum eigenvalue of ||(D^T D||). We initialize the algorithm with ||(S^0 = \{ s^0 \}||) where ||(s^0||) is the solution of unregularized problem (||(\lambda = 0||)) for a random sample.

We first simulate ISTA on given problem instances, which are parameterized by the parameter ||(x \in \mathcal{X} = [x_{\text{lb}}, x_{\text{ub}}]||). We randomly sample ||(x||) from uniform distribution over ||(\mathcal{X}||). The output of VP.solve(K=K) will be an array of size (n_samples, K) whose ||(n||)-th row is a list of infinity norm of residuals ||(s[k] - s[k-1]||) for ||(k=1,\ldots,K||).
